meta.program: The Task Sort · Take-Off Tuesday · Anchor's Edge · Vanderbilt
meta.audience: All Vanderbilt staff in the Anchor's Edge weekly rhythm; no management experience assumed. Works for 6 to 40 on a call; breakouts run in pairs. No prerequisites; April is the Spot AI-Exposed Work month.
meta.roomSetup: Virtual, instructor led: camera on, deck link in chat, breakouts of 2 available. Learners follow on their own screens via the welcome-slide link or QR. Nothing typed into the deck is saved or sent.
meta.postSession: Seven days out, send the pulse: 'Did the test on your card run? What did it teach you about the call? Which task gets sorted next?' Count of completed tests is the Level 3 metric for the month.

full.description: The full 45-minute virtual session: every interaction runs live, breakouts run in pairs, and the capstone gets read-alouds. The per-section minutes on each slide sum to 45 including transitions.

core.description: The 30-minute slot: agenda and core-idea slides pass in stride, breakouts become solo passes with chat share-outs, debriefs shrink to one voice. Never cut the section interactions or the capstone.

meta.framework: ATD facilitator-guide structure: per module SAY / DO / ASK (with anticipated responses) / DEBRIEF / TRANSITION, plus preparation checklists, materials, contingencies, and a tough-questions bank.
materials: Meeting platform with screen share and breakout rooms; deck link ready to paste in chat
Facilitator machine with the facilitator edition open; notifications off
Learners on their own devices with the learner link
Chat open for share-outs; the capstone copy button pastes there cleanly

weekBefore: Run the learner edition start to finish and do every interaction honestly; you will demo at least one live.
Read this month's theme page on the Anchor's Edge dashboard so the goal tie-in is fluent.
Send the invite with the learner link and one line on what to bring.
dayBefore: Test screen share with the facilitator edition; confirm the notes rail is readable.
Open the learner link on a second device; the QR must land there.
Run the section interactions once so you can drive them without reading.
thirtyMinBefore: Welcome slide up as people join; link pasted in chat.
Close every other tab; silence the machine.

contingencies.if: Screen share or the site fails mid-session
contingencies.then: Paste the learner link in chat and narrate from your own browser; every interaction runs on learner devices without the share.
Run the breakout prompts as 60-second chat storms: everyone types their answer at once, you read the best three aloud.

contingencies.if: Someone asks which specific AI tools are approved right now
contingencies.then: Point to the approved VU tools list on the Anchor's Edge dashboard rather than reciting from memory; the list moves, the traffic light does not.

contingencies.if: Someone insists their whole job should be left alone
contingencies.then: Agree that plenty of it may be, then ask for their most repetitive task and sort just that one together. One honest call usually unlocks the rest.

toughQuestions.q: If I automate parts of my job, am I automating myself out of it?
toughQuestions.a: The sort is per task, and no job is one task. Staff who can decompose, sort, and check their own work are exactly what Goal 3 calls workforce readiness; the freed hours move to the augment and leave-alone work where your judgment shows. The risk sits with unsorted weeks, and yours is sorted.

toughQuestions.q: My manager hasn't said anything about AI. Should I wait?
toughQuestions.a: Sorting your own week needs nobody's permission, and testing inside approved VU tools on green and yellow work is already within the rules. Share your sort with your manager afterward; Monday's session gave them a team-level version of this exact map, so you will be speaking the same language.

toughQuestions.q: How do I know if a task is yellow or red?
toughQuestions.a: Ask what the content is about. Internal but institutional, like meeting notes or draft plans: yellow, approved VU tools only. About an identifiable person, their health, performance, or circumstances: red, never. When a task mixes both, the red parts come out before any tool sees it, or the whole task stays human.

templates.title: Pre-work invite (paste into the calendar invite)
templates.body: Subject: Tuesday, 45 minutes on sorting your week before AI sorts it for you. Bring a rough sense of what last Tuesday was made of: the tasks, the outputs, the rhythms. Live and interactive; have the session link open on your own screen.

templates.title: 7-day pulse (send one week after)
templates.body: Subject: Did the test run? Three lines, reply whenever: 1) Did the test on your card run, in an approved VU tool? 2) What did it teach you about the call you made? 3) Which task gets sorted next?

sections.title: Welcome / QR
sections.purpose: Get everyone into the deck on their own screen and set the tone: 45 minutes, live, hands on.
sections.say: Welcome to Take-Off Tuesday. Scan the code or click the link in chat so this session runs on your screen too. Forty-five minutes, one focus: Task-decomposition: automate, augment, or leave alone.
facilitate: Slide up as people join; link pasted in chat every few minutes.
State the norm once: type into your own screen, nothing you enter is saved or sent.
sections.watchFor: People lurking without the deck open. The interactions only land if the deck is on their screen.
sections.transition: Before the topic, thirty seconds on why Vanderbilt is asking for this hour.

sections.title: The mission
sections.purpose: Anchor the session in the Chancellor's charge so the next 40 minutes read as mission work, not admin.
sections.say: This year of learning hangs off one sentence from the Chancellor: Vanderbilt will define the great university of the 21st Century and be it. Defining the great university of the 21st Century takes staff who redesign their own work instead of waiting for it to be redesigned. Every well-sorted week feeds Discovery and Innovation with hours that used to go to formatting.
facilitate: Read the mission line slowly, once.
Point at the tie-in line and let it sit; no discussion needed here.
sections.transition: That is the why. Here is the number we are moving.

sections.title: The goal we are targeting
sections.purpose: Name the enterprise goal this month serves.
sections.say: Every month of Anchor's Edge lands on one of three enterprise goals. This month is Goal 3, AI-Enabled Workforce Readiness: Equip managers to identify AI-exposed work, critical skills, and emerging talent needs on their teams, and translate those insights into practical workforce actions. Goal 3 counts on every staff member knowing which parts of their own work are AI-exposed. The task sort is how that knowledge gets made, one week at a time.
facilitate: Read the goal once, plainly.
One line, not a lecture: this session is one of the moves that serves it.
sections.transition: Here is what you will be able to do in 45 minutes.

sections.title: Objectives
sections.purpose: Set the contract for the session in under a minute.
sections.say: By the end of this session: break your working week into specific, repeatable tasks with outputs and rhythms; sort each task into automate, augment, or leave alone, and know the tells for each; test one sort call this week in an approved vu tool, checking step included. That is the whole contract.
facilitate: Read the three objectives briskly; do not elaborate yet.

sections.title: Agenda
sections.purpose: Show the path so the room can pace itself.
sections.say: Three stops: the decomposition, the three buckets, the first test. Each one has something to play with, so keep the deck open.
facilitate: Point once at each stop; ten seconds each.
sections.coreNote: Core: skip the read-through, gesture at the slide in passing.

sections.title: The decomposition
sections.purpose: Teach staff to turn the blur of a week into named tasks with outputs and rhythms.
sections.say: This month is about seeing what is changing in your work before it changes you, and the unit of change is never the job title. It is the task. So before any talk of AI, we do something older: write down what your week is actually made of, the way Tuesday actually went.
facilitate: Read the lead, then bring up the In the room card and let it land for a beat.
Run the discussion prompt: last Tuesday as three tasks. Take two or three voices on what was hardest to name.
Run the breakout: three real tasks, specific enough to picture.

ask.q: Why is it strangely hard to list your own tasks?
expect: We think in job titles and projects
Some will say their week never repeats
ask.respond: If a week truly never repeats, sort the parts that do: nearly every role carries a repeating core, and that core is where the sort pays off first.

sections.debrief: A sortable task has an output and a rhythm. That is the whole test, and most weeks hold ten of them once you look.
sections.watchFor: People writing job descriptions instead of tasks. Redirect: what did you produce, and how often does that repeat?
sections.transition: Tasks on the table. Now each one gets a call.
sections.coreNote: Core: skip the breakout; ask for one real task in chat instead.

sections.title: The three buckets
sections.purpose: Install the three calls and their tells, with the traffic light riding along on every sort.
sections.say: Three calls, and you make them per task, never per job. Automate: AI does it and you check every output. Augment: AI helps and you drive. Leave alone: human all the way. And every call rides the traffic light we share all year: green is public or generic, go; yellow is internal, approved VU tools only; red is private information about people, never.
facilitate: Run Make the call live; everyone plays on their own screen.
After the health-situation task, pause: ask why leave alone is the only call there.
Run the breakout: one task, one call, one challenge question.

ask.q: Which bucket do you expect will be smallest when you sort your own week?
expect: Some fear the leave-alone pile is shrinking
A few will say they have no idea yet
ask.respond: Most weeks sort mostly into augment, and the leave-alone pile is where your distinctly human value lives. Naming it is worth as much as the automation.

sections.debrief: Fixed format on public content leans automate. Internal drafting leans augment in approved VU tools. Trust, judgment, and people data stay human.
sections.watchFor: Anyone treating leave alone as failure or the lesser bucket. Reframe it: that pile is the case for the human in the role.
sections.transition: Calls made in your head are cheap. One of them earns a test.
sections.coreNote: Core: run the trainer, skip the breakout, take one voice on the debrief question.

sections.title: The first test
sections.purpose: Convert one sort call into a specific, checked, dated test in an approved VU tool.
sections.say: A sort that lives in your head is a nice opinion. It becomes a redesign of your week the first time you test a call: one task, one date, one approved tool, and a checking step with names on it. We are going to build that test now, and the checking step is the part people skip and regret.
facilitate: Run Set up the test; give the room two minutes for both choices.
Ask one volunteer to read their outcome aloud, weak or strong.
Point at the pattern: named task, named day, named check.

ask.q: Why does the checking step stay even when the tool has been right ten times in a row?
expect: The eleventh time is the one that ships wrong
The check is what makes automate safe
The output still carries your name
ask.respond: Right. Automate never means unattended. The output ships under your name, so the check is part of the task, permanently.

sections.debrief: The test formula: one task, one date, one approved tool, one named check. Small enough to run, real enough to teach.
sections.watchFor: Big-bang testers trying to automate a whole workflow at once. Shrink it: one task, this week.
sections.transition: Quick recap, then your own test goes on a card.
sections.coreNote: Core: everyone runs the builder solo; skip the read-aloud.

sections.title: The core idea
sections.purpose: Land the one sentence the session exists to install.
sections.say: If you keep one sentence from today, this is it. Read it once, out loud: AI never gets your job. It gets tasks, one at a time, and you make the call.
facilitate: Pause two beats after reading; the word animation carries it.
sections.coreNote: Core: pass through in stride; the sentence reads itself.

sections.title: Recap quiz
sections.purpose: Score the learning while it is fresh; wrong answers are teaching moments, not failures.
sections.say: Three questions, on your own screen. Answer honestly; the explanations are where the learning sticks.
facilitate: Give the room 90 seconds to run it individually.
Ask for a show of results in chat: how many got 3 of 3?
Read out the explanation for whichever question drew the most misses.
sections.watchFor: Rushing past the why lines. The explanations carry the teaching.
sections.transition: Now point it at your real week.

sections.title: Capstone commitment
sections.purpose: Convert the session into one named, dated action per person.
sections.say: Now make it real. One task from your actual week, the call you are testing, and the window it runs in. Task language only, no names of people. Build the card and copy it somewhere you will see it before the task next comes up. Two minutes, quiet, go.
facilitate: Two quiet minutes; everyone builds their own card.
Invite two or three volunteers to read their card aloud or paste it in chat.
Remind: copy the card somewhere you will see it this week.
sections.watchFor: Vague entries. Nudge for a name-able situation and a real date.

sections.title: Closing
sections.purpose: End with the next step and where this thread continues.
sections.say: You leave with your week in pieces and one test on the calendar, which is exactly where this month wants you. Thursday's Thrive Thursday gives you the other half of the skill: critical thinking that sorts AI hype from real value, so the claims about the next shiny tool meet three sharp questions before they meet your workflow. See you Thursday.
facilitate: Point at the next-step card; one sentence.
Name the rest of the week's rhythm: the other sessions echo this month's theme.
